policy.purpose: Source-bound research hypotheses for taxonomy refinement and later musician-reviewed style profiles.
not_evidence_of: permission to ingest or train on linked recordings, scores, or corpora

sources.title: Concert and Dance: the foundations of black jazz in South Africa between the twenties and the early forties
sources.limits: Historical analysis of early urban Black jazz and performance culture; does not define all later township jazz.

sources.title: Pennywhistle Kwela: A Musical, Historical and Socio-Political Analysis
sources.limits: A historically bounded thesis and corpus; not a universal rulebook for every later performance.

sources.title: Maskandi: a critical general inductive analysis of Zulu maskandi songs
sources.limits: Focuses particularly on introductory techniques; not an exhaustive account of all regional or contemporary variants.

sources.title: Music and Social Change in South Africa: Maskanda Past and Present
sources.limits: Historical, lyrical, and musical account; access and excerpt availability may be restricted.

sources.title: Something else is possible: transcultural collaboration as anti-apartheid activism in the music of Juluka
sources.limits: Discusses Maskanda in context of Juluka and related performance; not every Maskandi ensemble follows the described model.

sources.title: Religion, tradition and custom in a Zulu male vocal idiom
sources.limits: Strong context for one Zulu male vocal tradition and its performance culture; does not represent every contemporary choir.

sources.title: Nightsong: Performance, Power, and Practice in South Africa
sources.limits: Comprehensive performance and cultural study; source does not itself provide a machine-executable composition grammar.

sources.title: Sound of Africa! Making Music Zulu in a South African Studio
sources.limits: Focused studio ethnography of a Mbaqanga album and production process; avoid treating one production as exhaustive.

sources.title: Dancing to the beat of the diaspora: musical exchanges between Africa and its diasporas
sources.limits: Historical/style comparison; the cited account addresses particular phases and examples.

sources.title: Kwaito as history: Complicating contemporary historiographies
sources.limits: A historical argument about a changing, multivocal lineage; does not establish a universal production recipe.

sources.title: Kwaito's Promise: Music and the Aesthetics of Freedom in South Africa
sources.limits: Ethnographic and aesthetic study; avoid collapsing the genre into a single tempo, lyric, or political stance.

sources.title: A study of the linkages between popular music and politics in South Africa under Apartheid in the 1980s
sources.limits: Political and industry history of 1980s popular music; not a complete musical feature inventory.

sources.title: A history of Kwaito music
sources.limits: Useful historical context and influence map; not a compositional specification.

sources.title: Music and culture as forms of resistance
sources.limits: Public-history synthesis; not a substitute for primary or peer-reviewed analysis.

profiles.scope: Black South African electronic/popular dance music emerging in the 1990s; profile period and scene must be declared.
grounded_observations: A post-apartheid electronic/popular form with local and international influences, including house and earlier South African popular music.
Its histories are multivocal and non-linear; no single uncontested origin should be encoded.
Early vocal delivery includes a range from rhythmic speech to song; do not choose a single vocal mode.
candidate_discriminators: Period-conditioned house-adjacent loop and groove treatment.
Vocal continuum across speech, chant, sung refrain and response.
Local production, language and scene attributes alongside rather than replaced by international influence.
not_inferred: No universal BPM, drum pattern, key, language, lyric topic or political stance.
Not synonymous with South African house, gqom or amapiano.

profiles.scope: Zulu Maskandi/Maskanda song traditions, preserving solo, ensemble, regional and contemporary variants.
grounded_observations: The isihlabo instrumental introduction is predominant and important, while introductions can also involve concertina, bass guitar, voices and lead/group interplay.
Some documented ensemble practice uses an unmetered guitar introduction that lays out harmonic material, followed by a rhythmic/melodic guitar pattern and overlapping vocal/guitar response.
Fast guitar picking and blues-inflected vocal intonation are described in ethnomusicological work.
candidate_discriminators: Free/unmetered introductory guitar statement and its transition into the song groove.
Guitar as melodic, rhythmic and response voice rather than chordal backing only.
Picked ornament, multi-line guitar behavior and overlapping call-response.
not_inferred: No universal tuning, tempo, scale, lyric subject, or fixed ensemble.
Do not make the introductory passage a generic metronomic four-bar loop.
required_review: Regional/current practice review by Maskandi musicians

profiles.scope: Zulu a cappella choral and performance practice, including historically important male-voice ensembles and competition contexts.
grounded_observations: A cappella male-voice choral tradition associated with migrant workers and all-night competitions.
Close/cyclic harmony, a bass foundation, lead/group response and choreography are described in the sources.
Social, competitive, symbolic and movement practices form part of the performance context.
candidate_discriminators: Multi-part voice-leading and bass/upper-voice relationships.
Lead/choir timing, close-harmony movement, phrase releases and vocal attack.
Performance sequence and choreography represented independently from note sequence.
not_inferred: Not generic SATB chorale, barbershop or hymn arrangement.
Do not encode male-only as a universal present-day constraint.
Do not reduce the tradition to timbre alone.
required_review: Separate musical, vocal production, competition and movement schemas
Blind listening focused on ensemble phrasing

profiles.scope: Black South African urban popular/dance music; profile must identify historical period and specific use of the term.
grounded_observations: Documented later Mbaqanga combines driving dance pulse, cyclical harmony, short repeated/varied melody, independent bass/lead-guitar lines and vocal response.
A prominent studio ensemble profile has bass solo voice, soaring female-frontline harmony, electric guitar, bass, keyboard and drums.
Some educational and scholarly descriptions note close four-part vocal harmony, heavy bass, indlamu-derived drum impulse and layered/polyrhythmic activity.
candidate_discriminators: Bass/drum drive, rhythmic layering and independent melodic bass/guitar lines.
Short phrase units over a cyclic harmonic frame.
Period- and ensemble-specific lead/backing vocal architecture.
not_inferred: No single four-chord loop is universal.
Do not collapse 1940s African Jazz naming with later Mbaqanga studio/dance idioms.

profiles.scope: South African pennywhistle-led popular music, especially 1950s–early 1960s recorded and street-performance practices.
grounded_observations: Detailed analysis covers form, harmony, melody, rhythm, guitar, banjo, bass, drums, pennywhistle and saxophone.
Both swung and straight-beat repertoires are documented; their subdivision and historical relationships differ.
Lead melodic improvisation and secondary melodic/rhythmic lines are documented.
candidate_discriminators: Pennywhistle-led melodic improvisation and ornamentation, with historically scoped saxophone variants.
Explicit straight vs swung subdivision choice.
Interlocking banjo/guitar, bass and percussion roles.
not_inferred: Do not force every composition into swing or one fixed pennywhistle ensemble.
A pennywhistle instrument alone does not establish Kwela identity.

profiles.scope: Early urban Black South African dance music associated with Johannesburg slumyard/shebeen culture in the 1920s–1930s; later uses require separate scope.
grounded_observations: Keyboard/organ/piano, banjo and guitar styles built around repeated multi-bar harmonic cycles are described.
The basic four-measure I–IV–I6/4–V cycle is documented as a common pattern, with improvisatory melodic material over repetition.
Dance and extended social performance settings are central to public-history accounts.
candidate_discriminators: Repeating harmonic cycle with variable melodic improvisation.
Keyboard-led texture and guitar/banjo variants.
Extended dance form based on repetition, variation and performer interaction rather than verse/chorus.
not_inferred: A single progression is not universal.
No generic African scale, drum pattern or contemporary production palette should be inferred.
required_review: Period boundary and later revival treatment

profiles.scope: Ambiguous umbrella label; currently researched primarily through early/mid-20th-century urban Black South African jazz and Sophiatown/African Jazz histories.
grounded_observations: Early Black South African urban jazz-band and vaudeville traditions involved interaction among American jazz, local musical practices, venues and social histories.
Sophiatown-era bands performed swing-influenced music and contributed to new local idioms.
The literature distinguishes 1940s swing-influenced African Jazz from later Kwela and Mbaqanga developments.
candidate_discriminators: Period-specific band configuration and front-line/voice arrangement.
Swing-derived ensemble practice interacting with local melodic/rhythmic materials.
Sectional improvisation and ensemble riff behavior to be studied against actual repertoire.
not_inferred: Do not equate with all jazz made in townships, all South African jazz or contemporary township scenes.
Do not assign one big-band orchestration or one generic jazz grammar.
required_review: Naming and period review by South African jazz historians/performers
Decide rename, split, or umbrella/child hierarchy
Define representative repertory and arrangement scope

profiles.scope: Locally developed Black South African dance-pop discussed as bubblegum/township pop, especially in the 1980s; distinct from international Euro-American bubblegum.
grounded_observations: Energetic dance beats and township contexts are described.
Local bubblegum emerged through interaction of Mbaqanga histories and international pop/disco/house influences.
Programmed/sequenced synthetic timbres and vocal effects such as reverb, chorus and echo are described.
candidate_discriminators: Dance-oriented beat and hook/song form.
Studio/electronic production as part of identity, not merely an acoustic ensemble.
Local language and township-life materials alongside international pop influence.
not_inferred: Not generic international bubblegum, synthpop, disco or all 1980s South African popular music.
No fixed lyric language or political stance.
required_review: Separate local/international usage of bubblegum label
